prompt: Under IFRS 15, what is step 2 of the five-step model?

options.label: Identify the performance obligations in the contract
Determine the transaction price of the contract
Allocate the price to each separate obligation

explanation: The five steps: (1) identify the contract, (2) identify performance obligations, (3) determine the transaction price, (4) allocate it, (5) recognise revenue when/as each obligation is satisfied.

prompt: A company sells a machine plus 3 years of maintenance for one price. The maintenance is sold separately by others. How many performance obligations?

options.label: Two: the machine and the maintenance service
One: the contract is priced as a single bundle
Four: the machine plus one per maintenance year

explanation: A good or service is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and it is separately identifiable. Maintenance sold separately by others is distinct, so it is a separate obligation (a series satisfied over time).

prompt: A contract includes a bonus if the project finishes early. When can the bonus be included in the transaction price?

options.label: Only if a significant reversal is highly unlikely
Only once the bonus has been received in cash
Always, at its most likely amount from day one

explanation: Variable consideration is estimated (expected value or most likely amount) but constrained: it is included only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur.

prompt: Which is NOT one of the three criteria for recognising revenue over time under IFRS 15?

options.label: The customer has paid more than half of the price
The customer controls the asset as it is created
No alternative use plus an enforceable right to pay

explanation: Over-time criteria: (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits, (b) the customer controls the asset as it is created or enhanced, or (c) no alternative use plus an enforceable right to payment for work to date. Payment timing is not a criterion.

prompt: How is a non-current asset classified as held for sale measured under IFRS 5?

options.label: Lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell
Fair value less costs to sell, even if above carrying
Carrying amount, with depreciation continuing as usual

explanation: IFRS 5 measures held-for-sale assets at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell. Depreciation stops from the date of classification.

prompt: Management approves a plan to sell a building but will not start marketing it for 18 months. Is it held for sale?

options.label: No: it must be available and the sale highly probable
Yes: board approval alone is enough to classify it
Yes: classification only requires a sale within 24 months

explanation: Held-for-sale requires the asset to be available for immediate sale in its present condition and the sale to be highly probable, including an active programme to locate a buyer and completion expected within one year.

prompt: What happens to depreciation once an asset is classified as held for sale?

options.label: It stops from the date of classification
It continues until the sale actually completes
It is accelerated over the expected selling period

explanation: A non-current asset classified as held for sale (or part of a disposal group) is not depreciated or amortised.

prompt: A subsidiary that is a separate major line of business is classified as held for sale. How are its results shown in profit or loss?

options.label: As a single discontinued operations amount, post-tax
Line by line within continuing operations as usual
Directly in equity until the disposal is completed

explanation: A discontinued operation is a component that is a separate major line of business or geographical area. Its post-tax profit or loss (plus any remeasurement gain or loss) is presented as a single amount in the statement of profit or loss.

prompt: Which cost formula does IAS 2 prohibit?

options.label: LIFO (last in, first out)
FIFO (first in, first out)
Weighted average cost

explanation: IAS 2 permits FIFO and weighted average (and specific identification for non-interchangeable items). LIFO is not allowed.

prompt: Finished goods cost CHF 100. Expected selling price is CHF 110 and selling costs are CHF 15. What is the inventory carrying amount?

options.label: CHF 95 (net realisable value)
CHF 100 (historical cost)
CHF 110 (expected selling price)

explanation: Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value. NRV = 110 - 15 = 95, which is below cost of 100, so a write-down of 5 is recognised.

prompt: Which cost is excluded from the cost of inventories under IAS 2?

options.label: Abnormal amounts of wasted materials
Import duties that are not recoverable
Fixed production overheads at normal capacity

explanation: Costs of purchase include non-recoverable duties; conversion costs include fixed overheads allocated on normal capacity. Abnormal waste, most storage, admin overheads and selling costs are expensed.

prompt: Inventory written down to NRV last year has recovered in value. What do IAS 2 and FER 17 require?

options.label: Reverse the write-down, capped at original cost
Keep the write-down, reversals are prohibited
Revalue it up to the new, higher expected selling price

explanation: When the circumstances that caused the write-down no longer exist, the write-down is reversed, but only up to the original cost. Swiss GAAP FER 17 follows the same lower-of-cost-and-NRV logic.

prompt: How does a lessee account for most leases under IFRS 16?

options.label: Right-of-use asset and lease liability on balance sheet
Straight-line expense, nothing on the balance sheet
Finance or operating, depending on the transfer of risks and rewards

explanation: IFRS 16 removed the lessee operating/finance distinction: lessees recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for all leases, except optional exemptions for short-term and low-value leases.

prompt: Which lease can a lessee elect to keep off the balance sheet under IFRS 16?

options.label: A lease of 12 months or less with no purchase option
Any lease with payments below 5% of revenue
Any lease of property classified as operating

explanation: The recognition exemptions are short-term leases (12 months or less, no purchase option) and leases of low-value assets. Payments are then expensed straight-line.

prompt: At commencement, what discount rate does a lessee use for the lease liability if the implicit rate is not readily determinable?

options.label: The lessee's incremental borrowing rate
The central bank's risk-free policy rate
The lessor's weighted average cost of capital

explanation: Lease payments are discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease if readily determinable; otherwise at the lessee's incremental borrowing rate.

prompt: Which party still classifies leases as finance or operating under IFRS 16?

options.label: The lessor
The lessee
Both lessee and lessor

explanation: Lessor accounting is largely carried over from IAS 17: a lessor classifies each lease as finance (substantially all risks and rewards transferred) or operating.

prompt: Under IAS 38, how are research costs treated?

options.label: Always expensed in profit or loss as incurred
Capitalised when a product is likely to result
Capitalised and amortised over five years

explanation: No intangible asset arises from research; research expenditure is expensed. Development costs are capitalised only if all six IAS 38.57 criteria are met.

prompt: A brand built internally over 20 years has strong value. Can it be recognised as an asset?

options.label: No: internally generated brands cannot be recognised
Yes: at fair value if an expert valuation exists
Yes: at the cumulative amount of past marketing spend on the brand

explanation: Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles and customer lists cannot be recognised as intangible assets, because the cost cannot be distinguished from developing the business as a whole.

prompt: How is an intangible asset with an indefinite useful life treated?

options.label: Not amortised, but tested for impairment annually
Amortised over a maximum of 20 years
Amortised over 10 years unless a shorter life can be shown

explanation: Intangibles with indefinite useful lives are not amortised; they are tested for impairment at least annually and whenever there is an indication, and the indefinite-life assessment is reviewed each period.

prompt: How long is goodwill typically amortised under Swiss GAAP FER if it is capitalised?

options.label: Usually 5 years, in justified cases up to 20 years
It is never amortised, only tested for impairment
Exactly 40 years, on a straight-line basis

explanation: Under FER 30 goodwill can be offset against equity or capitalised and amortised, normally over 5 years and in justified cases up to 20 years. IFRS prohibits goodwill amortisation.

prompt: Which models can an entity choose for measuring a class of PP&E after recognition under IAS 16?

options.label: Cost model or revaluation model
Cost model or fair value through profit or loss
Revaluation model only, updated each year

explanation: IAS 16 allows the cost model or the revaluation model, applied to an entire class of PP&E. Revaluation surpluses go to OCI.

prompt: An aircraft has an engine that must be replaced every 5 years and a body that lasts 25. How is it depreciated?

options.label: Separately: each significant part on its own useful life
As one asset over the 25-year life of the body
As one asset over the 5-year life of the engine

explanation: Each part of PP&E with a cost significant to the total is depreciated separately (component approach).

prompt: Where does a revaluation increase on PP&E go, absent a previous decrease?

options.label: Other comprehensive income
Profit or loss, as a gain
Retained earnings

explanation: Revaluation increases are recognised in OCI and accumulated in a revaluation surplus, unless they reverse a decrease previously recognised in profit or loss.

prompt: A plant requires dismantling at the end of its life. How is the estimated dismantling cost treated at initial recognition?

options.label: Added to the asset's cost, with a matching provision
Expensed when the dismantling work actually takes place
Disclosed only, since it is decades in the future

explanation: The initial estimate of dismantling and site restoration costs is included in the cost of PP&E, with a corresponding provision under IAS 37.

prompt: How is the recoverable amount of an asset defined in IAS 36?

options.label: Higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use
Lower of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use (prudence)
Its carrying amount less accumulated depreciation

explanation: Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. An impairment loss arises when carrying amount exceeds it.

prompt: Which assets must be tested for impairment annually even without an indicator?

options.label: Goodwill and indefinite-life intangibles
All PP&E with a remaining life above ten years
Inventories and trade receivables

explanation: Goodwill, intangibles with indefinite useful lives and intangibles not yet available for use are tested at least annually, regardless of indicators.

prompt: An impairment loss on goodwill was recognised last year. The CGU's performance has now recovered. What happens?

options.label: Nothing: goodwill impairment is never reversed
Reverse it up to the original goodwill amount
Reverse it through OCI as a revaluation surplus

explanation: Impairment losses on other assets may be reversed if estimates change, but an impairment loss recognised for goodwill is never reversed.

prompt: A CGU with goodwill of 30 and other assets of 70 has a recoverable amount of 80. How is the loss of 20 allocated?

options.label: Entirely to goodwill, reducing it from 30 to 10
Pro rata: 6 to goodwill and 14 to other assets
Entirely to the other assets, protecting goodwill

explanation: An impairment loss for a CGU is allocated first to goodwill, then pro rata to the other assets based on their carrying amounts.

prompt: What two tests determine whether a debt instrument is measured at amortised cost under IFRS 9?

options.label: Business model test and SPPI cash-flow test
Credit rating test and active market test
Maturity test and intention-to-trade test

explanation: Amortised cost applies when the asset is held to collect contractual cash flows and those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI).

prompt: Which impairment model does IFRS 9 use for financial assets?

options.label: Expected credit loss model
Incurred loss model, based on loss events
Fair value loss model

explanation: IFRS 9 replaced the IAS 39 incurred loss model with an expected credit loss (ECL) model: 12-month ECL at stage 1, lifetime ECL once credit risk has increased significantly.

prompt: A company holds trade receivables without a significant financing component. Which ECL approach must it use?

options.label: Simplified approach: always lifetime expected losses
General approach: 12-month losses at first
No loss allowance until a customer actually defaults on payment

explanation: For trade receivables and contract assets without a significant financing component, IFRS 9 requires the simplified approach, recognising lifetime ECL from initial recognition (often via a provision matrix).

prompt: An entity irrevocably elects FVOCI for a strategic equity investment. What happens to gains on disposal?

options.label: They stay in equity, never recycled to profit or loss
They are reclassified to profit or loss when the shares are sold
They are split equally between OCI and profit

explanation: For equity investments designated at FVOCI, fair value changes go to OCI and are never recycled; only dividends go to profit or loss. The cumulative gain may be transferred within equity.

prompt: Which condition is NOT required to recognise a provision under IAS 37?

options.label: The amount must be known with certainty
A present obligation from a past event
A probable outflow of economic resources

explanation: A provision requires a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event, a probable outflow, and a reliable estimate. Certainty of amount is not required; that is what distinguishes provisions from other liabilities.

prompt: A retailer has a well-known policy of refunding unhappy customers, though not legally required. Should it recognise a provision?

options.label: Yes: the policy creates a constructive obligation
No: there is no legal obligation to refund
No: refunds are only recognised when paid

explanation: A constructive obligation arises from an established pattern of past practice that creates a valid expectation in others. The best estimate of refunds is provided for.

prompt: The board decides on a restructuring but has not announced it or started it. Can a provision be recognised?

options.label: No: a constructive obligation needs a plan and announcement
Yes: the board decision itself creates a constructive obligation
Yes: if the costs can be estimated reliably

explanation: A restructuring provision requires a detailed formal plan and a valid expectation in those affected, raised by starting to implement it or announcing its main features. A board decision alone is not enough.

prompt: How is a possible obligation whose outflow is not probable treated under IAS 37?

options.label: Disclosed as a contingent liability, unless remote
Recognised as a provision at its expected value
Ignored entirely until it becomes probable

explanation: Contingent liabilities are not recognised. They are disclosed unless the possibility of an outflow is remote.

prompt: Which method does IFRS 3 require for all business combinations?

options.label: The acquisition method (purchase accounting)
The pooling-of-interests method
The proportionate consolidation method

explanation: All business combinations within the scope of IFRS 3 are accounted for using the acquisition method.

prompt: How are acquisition-related costs such as legal and due diligence fees treated?

options.label: Expensed in profit or loss as incurred
Added to the goodwill recognised
Deducted directly from equity

explanation: Acquisition-related costs are expensed in the periods in which they are incurred, except costs to issue debt or equity securities.

prompt: An acquirer pays less than the fair value of net identifiable assets acquired. What is the first step?

options.label: Reassess identification and measurement of all items
Recognise the negative goodwill as a separate liability
Deduct the difference from the consideration paid

explanation: Before recognising a bargain purchase gain in profit or loss, the acquirer must reassess whether it has correctly identified and measured all assets, liabilities and the consideration.

prompt: How long is the measurement period for finalising provisional amounts in a business combination?

options.label: Up to one year from the acquisition date
Until the next annual financial statements
Up to three years from the acquisition date

explanation: Provisional amounts may be adjusted retrospectively during the measurement period, which cannot exceed one year from the acquisition date.

prompt: Which three elements define control under IFRS 10?

options.label: Power, exposure to variable returns, and linkage
Majority of shares, board seats, and veto rights
Ownership above 50%, influence, and dividends

explanation: An investor controls an investee when it has power over it, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use its power to affect those returns.

prompt: A parent owns 45% of an entity; the rest is held by thousands of small, unorganised shareholders. Could it have control?

options.label: Yes: de facto control can exist without a majority
No: control always requires more than 50%
No: it is an associate by definition at 45%

explanation: Power can arise from a large minority holding when other holdings are widely dispersed and unlikely to act together (de facto control).

prompt: How is a change in a parent's ownership in a subsidiary that does not result in loss of control treated?

options.label: As an equity transaction, with no gain or loss
As a partial disposal with gain in profit or loss
By remeasuring the entire subsidiary to fair value

explanation: Changes in ownership interests that do not result in a loss of control are equity transactions between owners.

prompt: Under Swiss GAAP FER 30, what alternative to capitalising goodwill exists?

options.label: Offsetting goodwill directly against equity
Expensing it fully in the year of acquisition
Recognising it in OCI and recycling it later

explanation: FER 30 allows goodwill to be offset against equity at acquisition, with the theoretical capitalisation and amortisation disclosed in the notes. IFRS does not permit this.

prompt: How does IFRS 13 define fair value?

options.label: An exit price between market participants
An entry price paid by the reporting entity
An entity-specific value in use estimate

explanation: Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date (exit price).

prompt: Which input is Level 1 in the IFRS 13 hierarchy?

options.label: Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets
Quoted prices for similar assets in active markets
Unobservable inputs from the entity's own data

explanation: Level 1: unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical items. Level 2: other observable inputs. Level 3: unobservable inputs.

prompt: A company owns land used as a factory, but a market participant would develop it as housing. What is the valuation premise?

options.label: Highest and best use from a participant's view
Current use by the entity, whatever the market
Lowest value use to remain prudent

explanation: The fair value of a non-financial asset reflects its highest and best use from the perspective of market participants, even if the entity uses it differently.

prompt: A fair value measurement relies on an internal cash-flow model with significant unobservable inputs. Which level?

options.label: Level 3
Level 2
Level 1

explanation: Measurements that depend significantly on unobservable inputs are Level 3 and require extra disclosures, including a reconciliation of movements.

prompt: Deferred tax under IAS 12 is based on which differences?

options.label: Temporary differences between carrying amount and tax base
Permanent differences between profit and taxable profit
Differences between current and prior year statutory tax rates

explanation: Deferred tax arises on temporary differences: the difference between the carrying amount of an asset or liability and its tax base.

prompt: An asset has a carrying amount of 100 and a tax base of 60. Tax rate is 20%. What arises?

options.label: A deferred tax liability of 8
A deferred tax asset of 8
A deferred tax liability of 20

explanation: Carrying amount above tax base for an asset is a taxable temporary difference of 40; at 20% that gives a deferred tax liability of 8.

prompt: When can a deferred tax asset for unused tax losses be recognised?

options.label: To the extent future taxable profit is probable
Always, as tax losses can be carried forward
Only when the losses are less than one year old

explanation: Deferred tax assets on unused losses are recognised only to the extent it is probable that future taxable profit will be available to use them.

prompt: At what tax rate are deferred taxes measured?

options.label: Rates expected when the difference reverses, if enacted
The current year's rate, regardless of future rates
The average rate of the last three financial years

explanation: Deferred tax is measured at the rates expected to apply when the asset is realised or liability settled, based on rates enacted or substantively enacted at the reporting date. Deferred tax is not discounted.

prompt: Which is NOT a component of a complete set of financial statements under IAS 1?

options.label: The management report on the business
The statement of changes in equity
The notes, including accounting policies

explanation: A complete set includes the statement of financial position, profit or loss and OCI, changes in equity, cash flows, notes, and comparatives. A management commentary is outside IAS 1.

prompt: A loan breaches a covenant at year end, making it repayable on demand. The bank grants a waiver after year end. How is it classified?

options.label: Current, since the waiver came after the reporting date
Non-current, since the waiver was eventually obtained
Split equally between current and non-current

explanation: If a covenant breach makes a liability payable on demand at the reporting date, it is current unless the lender agreed before the reporting date to a grace period of at least 12 months.

prompt: Which item of OCI is never reclassified to profit or loss?

options.label: Remeasurements of defined benefit plans
Translation differences on foreign operations
Effective portion of cash flow hedges

explanation: OCI is split into items that will not be reclassified (e.g. pension remeasurements, revaluation surplus) and items that may be (e.g. translation differences, cash flow hedges).

prompt: Can an entity offset a receivable from a customer against a payable to the same customer by default?

options.label: No: offsetting requires a specific IFRS to permit it
Yes: whenever both relate to the same counterparty
Yes: if the net figure is below materiality

explanation: Assets and liabilities, and income and expenses, are not offset unless required or permitted by an IFRS.

prompt: Which three categories does a statement of cash flows use?

options.label: Operating, investing and financing activities
Operating, capital and shareholder activities
Trading, non-trading and tax activities

explanation: IAS 7 and Swiss GAAP FER 4 classify cash flows into operating, investing and financing activities.

prompt: A company pays a lessor under IFRS 16. Where is the principal portion of the payment presented?

options.label: Financing activities
Operating activities
Investing activities

explanation: For lessees, payments of the principal portion of the lease liability are financing cash flows; interest follows the entity's policy for interest paid.

prompt: In the indirect method, how is depreciation treated?

options.label: Added back to profit, as it is a non-cash expense
Deducted from profit, as it reduces the carrying value of assets
Shown as an investing outflow for the year

explanation: Under the indirect method, profit is adjusted for non-cash items such as depreciation and for changes in working capital.

prompt: Which item usually qualifies as a cash equivalent under IAS 7?

options.label: A money market deposit maturing within three months
Listed shares that can be sold the same day
A five-year corporate bond that is redeemable on demand at par

explanation: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of value changes, typically with a maturity of three months or less. Equity investments are excluded.

prompt: What is an adjusting event after the reporting period?

options.label: Evidence of conditions that existed at the reporting date
Any event that happens before the auditor's report is signed
Conditions that arose after the reporting date but before issue

explanation: Adjusting events provide evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period. Non-adjusting events indicate conditions that arose afterwards.

prompt: A major customer that owed money at year end goes bankrupt in January. Is this adjusting?

options.label: Yes: it confirms the receivable was impaired at year end
No: the bankruptcy itself occurred after the reporting date
No: it is only disclosed as a subsequent event

explanation: Bankruptcy of a customer shortly after year end usually confirms a loss already existing on the receivable at the reporting date, so the receivable is adjusted.

prompt: Dividends are declared after year end but before the financial statements are authorised. How are they treated?

options.label: Not recognised as a liability, but disclosed
Recognised as a liability at the reporting date
Recognised directly as a reduction of equity

explanation: Dividends declared after the reporting period are not a present obligation at that date, so they are not recognised; they are disclosed in the notes.

prompt: What is the end point of the period IAS 10 covers?

options.label: The date the statements are authorised for issue
The date of the annual general meeting of the shareholders
The date the statements are filed publicly

explanation: Events after the reporting period are those between the end of the reporting period and the date the financial statements are authorised for issue.

prompt: When is a government grant recognised under IAS 20?

options.label: When compliance and receipt are reasonably assured
Only when the cash is actually received from the government
When the grant agreement is first signed

explanation: Grants are recognised when there is reasonable assurance that the entity will comply with the conditions and that the grant will be received.

prompt: A company receives a grant to buy a machine. Which presentations does IAS 20 allow?

options.label: Deferred income, or a deduction from the asset's cost
Immediate income in profit or loss on receipt
A direct credit to equity as a capital reserve

explanation: Grants related to assets are presented either as deferred income recognised over the asset's life, or deducted from the carrying amount of the asset.

prompt: A grant must be repaid because conditions were breached. How is the repayment treated?

options.label: As a change in accounting estimate, prospectively
As a prior period error, restating comparatives
As a change in accounting policy, retrospectively

explanation: A government grant that becomes repayable is accounted for as a change in accounting estimate.

prompt: How is the benefit of a below-market-rate government loan treated?

options.label: As a government grant, measured as the rate difference
Ignored: the loan is recorded at its face value
As interest income spread over the loan term

explanation: The benefit of a below-market loan is treated as a grant: the difference between the IFRS 9 initial carrying amount and the proceeds received.

prompt: Which borrowing costs must be capitalised under IAS 23?

options.label: Those directly attributable to a qualifying asset
All interest incurred by the entity during the year
Only interest on loans with a term above one year

explanation: Borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset are capitalised; others are expensed.

prompt: What is a qualifying asset under IAS 23?

options.label: An asset that takes a substantial time to get ready
Any asset financed by a specific bank loan
Any non-current asset above a size threshold

explanation: A qualifying asset necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.

prompt: Construction of a qualifying asset is suspended for six months due to a planning dispute. What happens to borrowing costs?

options.label: Capitalisation is suspended during that period
They continue to be capitalised as usual
Previously capitalised costs are reversed

explanation: Capitalisation is suspended during extended periods in which active development is suspended.

prompt: Funds borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset are temporarily invested. How is the investment income treated?

options.label: Deducted from the borrowing costs capitalised
Recognised as finance income in profit or loss
Added to the cost of the qualifying asset

explanation: For specific borrowings, borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation are the actual costs less any investment income on temporary investment of those borrowings.

prompt: Basic EPS is calculated as profit attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by what?

options.label: The weighted average number of ordinary shares
The number of shares at the reporting date
The number of shares authorised by the articles

explanation: Basic EPS uses the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period.

prompt: A bonus issue occurs during the year. How is it reflected in EPS?

options.label: Retrospectively, as if it happened at the start
Time-weighted from the date of the bonus issue
Ignored, as no cash was received for the shares

explanation: Bonus issues change the number of shares without a change in resources, so the shares are treated as outstanding from the start of the earliest period presented.

prompt: Which potential shares are excluded from diluted EPS?

options.label: Antidilutive ones that would increase EPS
Share options that are currently out of the money
Convertible bonds issued during the year

explanation: Potential ordinary shares are included only if dilutive; antidilutive potential shares are excluded.

prompt: Which entities must present EPS under IAS 33?

options.label: Those whose ordinary shares are publicly traded
All entities that prepare IFRS statements
Only banks and insurance companies

explanation: IAS 33 applies to entities whose ordinary shares are publicly traded or in the process of being issued in public markets.

prompt: Which shareholding presumes significant influence under IAS 28?

options.label: 20% or more of the voting power
50% or more of the voting power
10% or more of the share capital

explanation: Holding 20% or more of voting power presumes significant influence unless clearly demonstrated otherwise.

prompt: How are associates accounted for in consolidated statements?

options.label: Using the equity method
Using full consolidation
At fair value through OCI

explanation: Investments in associates and joint ventures are accounted for using the equity method.

prompt: An investor sells inventory to its 30% associate at a profit. The associate still holds it at year end. What happens?

options.label: 30% of the unrealised profit is eliminated
The full amount of the unrealised profit is eliminated
No elimination, as it is a third party

explanation: Profits from upstream and downstream transactions with an associate are eliminated to the extent of the investor's interest in the associate.

prompt: An associate's losses exceed the investor's carrying amount. What does the investor do?

options.label: Stops recognising losses unless it has an obligation
Recognises a liability for the full excess losses
Reverses the equity method from inception

explanation: Once the interest is reduced to zero, further losses are recognised only to the extent of legal or constructive obligations or payments made on the associate's behalf.

prompt: Where are remeasurements of a net defined benefit liability recognised?

options.label: Other comprehensive income
Profit or loss
Directly in retained earnings

explanation: Remeasurements (actuarial gains and losses, return on plan assets excluding interest) are recognised in OCI and never reclassified.

prompt: A Swiss company has a BVG/LPP pension plan. How does Swiss GAAP FER 16 differ from IAS 19?

options.label: FER 16 relies on the plan's Swiss GAAP FER 26 accounts
FER 16 requires the same projected unit credit method
FER 16 forbids recognising any pension liabilities

explanation: FER 16 assesses economic benefits or obligations based on the pension fund's statements prepared under FER 26, rather than an IAS 19 projected unit credit valuation. IFRS reporters often show significant net liabilities for Swiss plans.

prompt: Which actuarial method does IAS 19 require for defined benefit obligations?

options.label: The projected unit credit method
The entry age normal cost method
The accrued benefit cost method

explanation: IAS 19 requires the projected unit credit method to measure the present value of defined benefit obligations.

prompt: At what rate is a defined benefit obligation discounted under IAS 19?

options.label: High quality corporate bond yields
The entity's own borrowing rate
The expected return on plan assets

explanation: The discount rate is determined by market yields on high quality corporate bonds (or government bonds where there is no deep market), consistent with the currency and term.

prompt: How are monetary items in foreign currency translated at the reporting date?

options.label: At the closing rate
At the historical rate
At the average rate

explanation: Foreign currency monetary items are translated at the closing rate; non-monetary items at cost use the historical rate.

prompt: Where do exchange differences on translating a foreign operation into the presentation currency go?

options.label: OCI, recycled on disposal of the operation
Profit or loss in the period they arise
Retained earnings, never recycled

explanation: Translation differences are recognised in OCI and accumulated in a separate equity component, reclassified to profit or loss on disposal of the foreign operation.

prompt: A Swiss subsidiary sells mainly in euros, sets prices in euros and pays most costs in euros. What is its functional currency?

options.label: The euro, as the main economic driver
The Swiss franc, as the local currency
The group's reporting currency

explanation: Functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment, driven mainly by the currency that influences sales prices and costs.

prompt: A company prepays a supplier in USD for goods to be delivered later. How is the prepayment translated at year end?

options.label: At the historical rate, as a non-monetary item
At the closing rate, as it is a monetary item payable in USD
At the average rate for the year

explanation: Prepayments for goods or services are non-monetary items and remain at the exchange rate on the date of the advance consideration.

prompt: Which is a related party of a reporting entity under IAS 24?

options.label: A close family member of a key manager
A major customer providing 30% of sales
A bank that lends to the entity

explanation: Related parties include key management personnel and their close family members. Major customers, suppliers and finance providers are not related parties merely through economic dependence.

prompt: An entity sells goods to a related party at normal market prices. Is disclosure still required?

options.label: Yes: the transactions and balances are disclosed
No: arm's length transactions are exempt
No: only loans to directors are disclosed

explanation: Related party transactions are disclosed whether or not a price is charged and regardless of whether terms are at arm's length.

prompt: Which key management personnel information must be disclosed in total?

options.label: Their compensation, by category
Their private shareholdings
Their personal tax returns

explanation: IAS 24 requires disclosure of key management personnel compensation in total and by category (short-term, post-employment, other long-term, termination, share-based).

prompt: Can an entity state that related party transactions were at arm's length?

options.label: Only if that can be substantiated
Always, as it is a standard statement
Never, it is forbidden by IAS 24

explanation: Disclosures that related party transactions were made on terms equivalent to arm's length transactions are made only if such terms can be substantiated.

prompt: How is an equity-settled share-based payment to employees measured?

options.label: Fair value of the equity instruments at grant date
Fair value of the shares at each reporting date
Intrinsic value at the vesting date

explanation: Equity-settled awards to employees are measured at grant-date fair value and not remeasured.

prompt: An award vests only if the share price reaches CHF 50. The target is missed. Is the expense reversed?

options.label: No: market conditions are reflected in grant-date fair value
Yes: no shares vest, so the full cumulative expense is reversed
Yes: half of the cumulative expense is reversed on forfeiture

explanation: Market conditions are taken into account in the grant-date fair value; the expense is recognised if all non-market conditions are met, even if the market condition is not.

prompt: How is a cash-settled share-based payment liability measured?

options.label: At fair value, remeasured at each reporting date
At grant-date fair value, not remeasured
At the nominal amount of the shares

explanation: Cash-settled awards create a liability remeasured to fair value at each reporting date and at settlement, with changes in profit or loss.

prompt: Employees must stay three years for options to vest. Over what period is the expense recognised?

options.label: Over the three-year vesting period
In full on the grant date
In full when the options are exercised

explanation: When there is a service condition, the expense is recognised over the vesting period as services are received.

prompt: Which approach does IFRS 8 use to identify operating segments?

options.label: The management approach, based on internal reporting
The risk-and-return approach by product type
The legal entity approach by subsidiary

explanation: Segments are identified based on internal reports reviewed by the chief operating decision maker.

prompt: Which threshold makes an operating segment reportable?

options.label: 10% of revenue, profit or loss, or assets
5% of revenue, with no profit or asset test
25% of total equity or of total liabilities

explanation: A segment is reportable if its revenue, absolute profit or loss, or assets are 10% or more of the combined amounts.

prompt: Reportable segments make up only 60% of external revenue. What must the entity do?

options.label: Add segments until they reach at least 75%
Nothing: 60% is above the 50% minimum
Merge every segment into a single one

explanation: If reportable segments' external revenue is below 75% of total, additional segments are identified as reportable until 75% is reached.

prompt: Which entities must apply IFRS 8?

options.label: Those whose debt or equity is publicly traded
All entities that have more than one subsidiary
All entities above a revenue threshold

explanation: IFRS 8 applies to entities whose debt or equity instruments are traded in a public market or that are filing to issue them.

prompt: What are the two types of joint arrangement under IFRS 11?

options.label: Joint operations and joint ventures
Joint ventures and associates
Joint control and joint influence

explanation: Joint arrangements are either joint operations (rights to assets, obligations for liabilities) or joint ventures (rights to net assets).

prompt: How does a joint operator account for its interest?

options.label: Its share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses
Using the equity method on its net investment in the arrangement
At fair value through profit or loss

explanation: A joint operator recognises its own assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses, including its share of those held or incurred jointly.

prompt: Two companies set up a separate vehicle; its legal form gives them rights only to net assets, with no other terms. What is it?

options.label: A joint venture, using the equity method
A joint operation, line by line
A subsidiary of each of the two parties

explanation: When a separate vehicle's legal form, contractual terms and other facts give parties rights to net assets, the arrangement is a joint venture, accounted for using the equity method.

prompt: What does joint control require?

options.label: Unanimous consent on decisions about relevant activities
Each party holding exactly 50% of the votes
A majority vote of the parties to the arrangement

explanation: Joint control is the contractually agreed sharing of control, existing only when decisions about relevant activities require unanimous consent of the parties sharing control.

prompt: In an integrated audit under AS 2201, what does the auditor opine on besides the financial statements?

options.label: The effectiveness of internal control over reporting
Management's forecasts and its business strategy
The efficiency of the entity's operating processes

explanation: An integrated audit includes an opinion on ICFR effectiveness as of year end, alongside the financial statement opinion.

prompt: Which approach does AS 2201 require for selecting controls to test?

options.label: Top-down approach starting at the entity level
Bottom-up approach starting with transactions
Random selection across all business processes

explanation: The auditor uses a top-down approach: begin at the financial statement level and entity-level controls, then work down to significant accounts, assertions and relevant controls.

prompt: Under ISA, when must the auditor test the operating effectiveness of controls?

options.label: When relying on them, or if substantive work is not enough
Always, for every control identified as relevant to the audit
Never, as ISA audits are purely substantive

explanation: Controls are tested when the risk assessment expects them to operate effectively (the auditor plans to rely on them), or when substantive procedures alone cannot give sufficient appropriate evidence.

prompt: Controls were tested last year and nothing has changed. How often can reliance continue without retesting under ISA 330?

options.label: At least once every third audit, some each year
Indefinitely, as long as the controls and the systems do not change
Never: all controls must be retested every year

explanation: The auditor may rely on prior-period evidence for unchanged controls, but must test them at least once every third audit, and test some controls each year. Controls over significant risks are tested in the current period.

prompt: Under ISA 315 (Revised 2019), what are the two components of the risk of material misstatement?

options.label: Inherent risk and control risk
Detection risk and sampling risk
Business risk and engagement risk

explanation: RMM at the assertion level consists of inherent risk and control risk, which ISA 315 (Revised 2019) requires to be assessed separately.

prompt: What is the inherent risk spectrum in ISA 315 (Revised 2019)?

options.label: A range from lower to higher, by likelihood and size
A fixed scale of five levels set by regulators
A binary split between significant and normal risk

explanation: Inherent risk is assessed on a spectrum depending on the likelihood and magnitude of misstatement; significant risks sit at the upper end.

prompt: Which risk is presumed to be significant in every audit under ISA?

options.label: Management override of controls
Valuation of property, plant and equipment
Completeness of trade payables

explanation: The risk of management override of controls is present in all entities and is treated as a significant risk. Revenue recognition fraud risk is also presumed, but that presumption can be rebutted.

prompt: Which is one of the inherent risk factors listed in ISA 315 (Revised 2019)?

options.label: Complexity
Profitability
Audit fee

explanation: The inherent risk factors are complexity, subjectivity, change, uncertainty, and susceptibility to misstatement due to management bias or fraud.

prompt: What is the overall objective of the auditor under ISA 200?

options.label: Reasonable assurance of no material misstatement
Absolute assurance that no fraud or error has occurred during the year
Confirmation that management ran the business well

explanation: The auditor aims to obtain reasonable assurance that the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to report accordingly.

prompt: Why can an audit never give absolute assurance?

options.label: Because of the inherent limitations of an audit
Because auditors are not independent of clients
Because audit fees are capped by regulation

explanation: Inherent limitations (judgement, the nature of evidence, possible collusion or override, timing) mean evidence is persuasive rather than conclusive.

prompt: What attitude does ISA 200 require the auditor to maintain throughout the audit?

options.label: Professional scepticism
Presumed management dishonesty
Full trust in management

explanation: Professional scepticism is a questioning mind, alert to conditions indicating possible misstatement. It neither assumes dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty.

prompt: The 'preconditions for an audit' under ISA 210 include which of these?

options.label: Management accepts responsibility for the statements
The auditor has audited the client for five years
The client has no going concern doubts at all

explanation: Preconditions include an acceptable financial reporting framework and management's agreement that it is responsible for the statements, internal control, and providing access.

prompt: By when must the final audit file be assembled under ISA 230?

options.label: Usually within 60 days after the report date
Within 7 days after the date of the auditor's report
Before the auditor's report is dated

explanation: ISQM 1 requires timely assembly; an appropriate time limit is ordinarily not more than 60 days after the date of the auditor's report.

prompt: Which test describes how detailed audit documentation must be?

options.label: An experienced auditor with no link must understand it
The client's CFO must be able to follow every step
A regulator must be able to reperform all work

explanation: Documentation must enable an experienced auditor, with no previous connection to the audit, to understand the procedures, results, evidence and significant judgements.

prompt: After the file is assembled, a manager wants to delete an old draft working paper. Is this allowed?

options.label: No: nothing may be deleted before retention ends
Yes: drafts are not part of the final file
Yes: as long as the engagement partner approves the deletion

explanation: After assembly, the auditor must not delete or discard documentation of any nature before the end of its retention period. Superseded drafts should be removed before assembly is completed.

prompt: New information requires adding work to the file after the report date. What must be documented?

options.label: The reasons, the work done, who did it and when
Nothing, as long as the opinion is unchanged
Only the partner's sign-off on the new work

explanation: When documentation is modified or added after assembly, the auditor documents the specific reasons, and when and by whom the changes were made and reviewed.

prompt: Which two types of intentional misstatement does ISA 240 cover?

options.label: Fraudulent reporting and misappropriation of assets
Errors in estimates and errors in disclosures
Tax evasion and breaches of regulations

explanation: ISA 240 deals with fraudulent financial reporting and misappropriation of assets.

prompt: What are the three conditions of the fraud triangle?

options.label: Pressure, opportunity, and rationalisation
Motive, means, and lack of evidence
Greed, weak controls, and complex systems

explanation: Fraud risk factors are typically grouped into incentives or pressures, opportunities, and attitudes or rationalisations.

prompt: Which procedure is always required to respond to management override risk?

options.label: Testing journal entries and other adjustments
Confirming all bank accounts with third parties
Attending the physical inventory count

explanation: Regardless of risk assessment, the auditor tests journal entries, reviews accounting estimates for bias, and evaluates the rationale for significant unusual transactions.

prompt: The engagement team holds a discussion on fraud risks. When should it take place?

options.label: During planning, with key team members involved
Only after a fraud has actually been detected
At the end of the audit, before signing off

explanation: ISA 240 and ISA 315 require a team discussion on how and where the financial statements may be susceptible to material misstatement due to fraud.

prompt: To whom must significant deficiencies in internal control be communicated in writing?

options.label: Those charged with governance
The tax authorities
All employees of the entity

explanation: Significant deficiencies are communicated in writing to those charged with governance on a timely basis, and to management.

prompt: Under AS 2201, what is a material weakness?

options.label: A deficiency that could reasonably lead to a material misstatement
Any control failure identified during the audit, regardless of size
A deficiency that has already caused an actual financial loss

explanation: A material weakness is a deficiency, or combination of deficiencies, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis.

prompt: Does the absolute size of a misstatement found determine whether a deficiency is significant?

options.label: No: what matters is what could happen, not what did
Yes: only deficiencies causing errors count
Yes: only errors above materiality count

explanation: Significance depends on the potential for misstatement, not on whether a misstatement actually occurred.

prompt: If a material weakness exists at year end, what ICFR opinion does AS 2201 require?

options.label: An adverse opinion on ICFR
A qualified opinion on ICFR
An unmodified opinion with an emphasis

explanation: If one or more material weaknesses exist, the auditor must express an adverse opinion on the company's internal control over financial reporting.

prompt: What is performance materiality under ISA 320?

options.label: An amount below materiality to cover aggregate misstatement
The materiality level used for the ICFR opinion only
A threshold for misstatements that are clearly trivial

explanation: Performance materiality is set below overall materiality to reduce to an appropriately low level the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements exceed materiality.

prompt: Can materiality be set lower for particular classes of transactions or disclosures?

options.label: Yes, where users would be influenced by smaller amounts
No: one single materiality applies to every item
Only for listed entities, where required by the securities regulators

explanation: Specific materiality levels may be set for items where misstatements of lesser amounts could reasonably influence users, such as related party transactions or key management pay.

prompt: During fieldwork, actual results come in much lower than the forecasts used to set materiality. What should the auditor do?

options.label: Revise materiality and reconsider the procedures
Keep materiality, as it is set only at planning
Withdraw from the engagement immediately

explanation: Materiality is revised when the auditor becomes aware of information that would have caused a different amount initially, and the auditor considers whether the nature and extent of procedures remain appropriate.

prompt: What does ISA 450 require for misstatements below the clearly trivial threshold?

options.label: They need not be accumulated
They must be corrected by management
They are reported to the regulator

explanation: The auditor accumulates misstatements identified during the audit, other than those that are clearly trivial.

prompt: Which source of evidence is generally the most reliable under ISA 500?

options.label: Evidence obtained directly from an independent source
Evidence provided by the client in photocopy
Evidence obtained through oral client inquiry

explanation: Evidence from independent external sources, obtained directly by the auditor and in documentary original form, is generally more reliable than internally generated or indirect evidence.

prompt: Is inquiry alone sufficient appropriate evidence to test operating effectiveness of controls?

options.label: No: it must be combined with other procedures
Yes: if the inquiry is made of senior management and the CFO
Yes: as long as the answers are documented in writing

explanation: Inquiry alone is not sufficient to test operating effectiveness; it must be combined with observation, inspection or reperformance.

prompt: Which procedure best tests the existence assertion for receivables?

options.label: Sending external confirmations to customers
Reviewing credit notes issued after year end
Recalculating the ageing of the receivables

explanation: External confirmations from customers give direct third-party evidence that the receivable exists.

prompt: The client refuses to let the auditor send a confirmation to a key customer. What must the auditor do?

options.label: Ask why, evaluate it, and perform alternative procedures
Accept the refusal and remove the balance from testing
Send the confirmation anyway without telling the client

explanation: The auditor inquires about management's reasons, seeks evidence of their validity and reasonableness, assesses fraud risk implications, and performs alternative procedures.

prompt: When inventory is material, what does ISA 501 require?

options.label: Attending the physical count, unless impracticable
Confirming inventory balances with all suppliers
Hiring an expert to value inventory every year

explanation: If inventory is material, the auditor attends the physical count (unless impracticable) and performs procedures on the final records.

prompt: What does ISA 501 require regarding litigation and claims?

options.label: Procedures to identify them, often lawyer inquiry
Only a review of the legal expense account for unusual items
No procedures: it is management's area

explanation: The auditor designs procedures to identify litigation and claims, including inquiry of management and in-house counsel and review of legal expense accounts, and seeks direct communication with external legal counsel when a risk exists.

prompt: Which assertion is mainly tested by tracing goods received notes to the purchases ledger?

options.label: Completeness
Existence
Presentation

explanation: Tracing from source documents into the records tests completeness; vouching from records to supporting documents tests occurrence or existence.

prompt: Inventory count attendance is impracticable due to the nature of the site. What must the auditor do?

options.label: Perform alternative procedures to obtain evidence
Issue a disclaimer of opinion automatically for the whole audit
Rely on management's own count results alone

explanation: If attendance is impracticable, the auditor performs alternative procedures (e.g. inspecting subsequent sales documentation). If that is not possible, the auditor modifies the opinion.

prompt: At which stage are analytical procedures required under ISA 520?

options.label: Near the end, to form an overall conclusion
Only during the planning stage, as a risk assessment tool
Only as substantive tests of detail

explanation: ISA 520 requires analytical procedures near the end of the audit to form an overall conclusion; ISA 315 also requires them at risk assessment.

prompt: What must be done when a substantive analytical procedure shows a difference above the threshold?

options.label: Investigate it with inquiry and further evidence
Accept it as long as the difference is below overall materiality
Record the full difference as a known misstatement

explanation: The auditor investigates by inquiring of management and obtaining corroborating evidence, and performs other procedures as necessary.

prompt: Which factor makes a substantive analytical procedure more reliable?

options.label: Disaggregated data from independent sources
Highly aggregated data from management
Data prepared after the year end by sales staff

explanation: Reliability increases with disaggregated data, data from independent sources, and data subject to effective controls.

prompt: Gross margin is stable at 40% while the industry fell to 30%. What is the best response?

options.label: Treat it as an unusual relationship to investigate
Conclude that the client is simply very efficient
Ignore it, since a stable margin is a good sign

explanation: An unexpected relationship with industry data can indicate misstatement (e.g. revenue cut-off or inventory overstatement) and must be investigated.

prompt: What is sampling risk under ISA 530?

options.label: The risk that a sample leads to a different conclusion
The risk that the auditor uses an unsuitable procedure
The risk that the client manipulates the sample

explanation: Sampling risk is the risk that the auditor's conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion if the entire population were tested. Non-sampling risk covers other causes.

prompt: A sample item is lost and alternative procedures are impossible. How is it treated?

options.label: As a misstatement or control deviation
Replaced by another item chosen at random
Ignored and excluded from the sample results

explanation: If the auditor cannot apply the procedure or suitable alternatives to a selected item, it is treated as a deviation or misstatement.

prompt: Which method gives every item an equal chance of selection?

options.label: Random selection
Block selection
Judgemental selection

explanation: Random selection (e.g. with random number generators) gives each sampling unit a known chance of selection. Haphazard and block selection do not meet that standard as cleanly.

prompt: An error found in a sample is clearly isolated and not representative. Can it be excluded from projection?

options.label: Only in extremely rare cases, with high certainty
Yes: isolated errors never need to be projected
Yes: if management corrects it before sign-off

explanation: An anomaly can be excluded only in extremely rare circumstances, after obtaining a high degree of certainty that it is not representative of the population.

prompt: ISA 540 (Revised) bases its risk assessment for estimates on which factors?

options.label: Estimation uncertainty, complexity, subjectivity
Materiality, sample size, and the timing of fieldwork procedures
Profitability, liquidity, and leverage

explanation: ISA 540 (Revised) requires the auditor to consider the degree to which estimation uncertainty, complexity, subjectivity and other inherent risk factors affect the risk of misstatement.

prompt: What does the auditor do when reviewing the outcome of prior-year estimates?

options.label: Compare them to actual outcomes to inform risk assessment
Correct the prior year's financial statements for any difference
Nothing, as only current-year estimates matter

explanation: The retrospective review helps identify management bias and the effectiveness of past estimation; it is not meant to question judgements made on information available at the time.

prompt: Which is one of the three ISA 540 approaches to respond to estimation risks?

options.label: Developing an auditor's point estimate or range
Accepting management's estimate if signed by the CFO
Asking the client's lawyer to approve the estimate

explanation: The auditor obtains evidence from events up to the report date, tests how management made the estimate, or develops its own point estimate or range.

prompt: Each estimate is reasonable alone, but all of them push profit up. What should the auditor consider?

options.label: Possible management bias in the estimates as a whole
Nothing: each estimate is individually acceptable
A material misstatement must be recorded immediately

explanation: Indicators of possible management bias, even if individual estimates are reasonable, must be evaluated, including their effect on the audit and fraud risk.

prompt: Why are related parties a specific audit focus under ISA 550?

options.label: They may enable fraud and transactions off normal terms
They are always illegal under company law
They must be disclosed in the auditor's report

explanation: Related party relationships may present greater risk of material misstatement, including through fraud, because they can be complex and not at arm's length.

prompt: The auditor finds a related party management did not disclose. What must happen?

options.label: Inform the team, identify its deals, reassess risk
Note it in the file and address it in next year's audit planning
Disclose it directly to shareholders at the next general meeting

explanation: The auditor promptly communicates it to the team, asks management to identify all transactions with it, performs procedures and reconsiders the risk of other undisclosed related parties, including fraud.

prompt: Which significant transactions require the auditor to inspect contracts under ISA 550?

options.label: Related party ones outside the normal course
All sales above the materiality threshold
Every transaction approved by the board

explanation: For significant related party transactions outside the normal course of business, the auditor inspects contracts and evaluates their business rationale and authorisation.

prompt: Management states related party sales were at arm's length. What must the auditor do?

options.label: Obtain sufficient appropriate evidence to support it
Accept it through the written representation letter alone
Recompute every sale using market prices

explanation: If management asserts arm's length terms, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate evidence about that assertion.

prompt: Until when must the auditor actively search for subsequent events under ISA 560?

options.label: Up to the date of the auditor's report
Up to the date of the annual general meeting
Up to the end of the following quarter

explanation: The auditor performs procedures covering the period from the financial statement date to the date of the auditor's report.

prompt: After the report is signed but before issue, the auditor learns of a fact that would have changed it. What now?

options.label: Discuss with management and consider an amendment
Nothing: the auditor has no duty after signing
Withdraw the report and resign at once

explanation: The auditor has no obligation to search after the report date, but if it becomes aware of such a fact, it discusses it with management, determines whether amendment is needed, and acts accordingly.

prompt: Which procedure is typical for subsequent events?

options.label: Reading minutes of meetings held after year end
Recalculating depreciation for the year
Confirming opening balances with the predecessor

explanation: Procedures include inquiry of management, reading minutes of meetings held after the period end, and reading the latest interim financial statements.

prompt: Statements are amended after issue for a newly discovered fact. What does the auditor do?

options.label: Issue a new report including an emphasis of matter
Reissue the original report keeping its original date
Nothing: the issued report stands as before

explanation: The auditor audits the amendment, extends procedures to the new report date, and issues a new auditor's report with an emphasis of matter or other matter paragraph referring to the amendment.

prompt: Over what minimum period must management assess going concern under IAS 1?

options.label: At least 12 months from the reporting date
At least 12 months from the date of the report
At least 24 months from the reporting date

explanation: IAS 1 requires management to consider at least 12 months from the end of the reporting period. ISA 570 asks the auditor to request an extension if management covers less.

prompt: A material uncertainty on going concern exists and is properly disclosed. What is the opinion?

options.label: Unmodified, with a material uncertainty section
Qualified, because of the uncertainty over going concern
Adverse, because of the uncertainty

explanation: If adequately disclosed, the auditor issues an unmodified opinion and includes a 'Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern' section.

prompt: Statements are prepared on a going concern basis, but liquidation is the auditor's conclusion. What opinion?

options.label: Adverse opinion
Qualified opinion
Unmodified opinion

explanation: If the going concern basis is inappropriate, the auditor expresses an adverse opinion.

prompt: Which is a financial indicator of going concern doubt in ISA 570?

options.label: Net liability or net current liability position
A change in the entity's accounting policies
A large dividend paid in the prior year

explanation: Examples include net liabilities, fixed-term loans near maturity without realistic renewal, negative operating cash flows, and substantial operating losses.

prompt: Which opinion is given when misstatements are material but not pervasive?

options.label: Qualified opinion
Adverse opinion
Disclaimer of opinion

explanation: Material but not pervasive: qualified. Material and pervasive misstatement: adverse. Inability to obtain evidence, possibly pervasive: disclaimer.

prompt: Which entities must communicate key audit matters under ISA 701?

options.label: Listed entities, and others when required
All entities, without any exception
Only entities with a modified opinion

explanation: KAMs are required for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, and where required by law or chosen voluntarily.

prompt: The auditor cannot obtain evidence for an area that could be material and pervasive. What opinion?

options.label: Disclaimer
Adverse
Qualified

explanation: When unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence and the possible effects could be both material and pervasive, the auditor disclaims an opinion.

prompt: When is an emphasis of matter paragraph used?

options.label: To highlight a properly disclosed matter key to users
To flag a misstatement that management refused to correct before issue
To replace the opinion when evidence is missing

explanation: An emphasis of matter draws attention to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed that is fundamental to users' understanding. It does not modify the opinion.

prompt: Which standard requires a firm to design a system of quality management?

options.label: ISQM 1
ISA 220
ISA 600

explanation: ISQM 1 addresses the firm's system of quality management. ISA 220 (Revised) covers quality management at the engagement level.

prompt: Who takes overall responsibility for quality on an audit engagement under ISA 220 (Revised)?

options.label: The engagement partner
The engagement quality reviewer
The audit committee chair

explanation: The engagement partner takes overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality on the engagement, with sufficient and appropriate involvement throughout.

prompt: Which engagements must have an engagement quality review under ISQM 1?

options.label: Audits of listed entities, among others
Every audit, regardless of the client or its size
Only audits with a modified opinion

explanation: ISQM 1 requires an EQR for audits of listed entities, engagements where law or regulation requires one, and others the firm determines appropriate in response to quality risks.

prompt: The partner who led a listed client's audit until last year wants to be its engagement quality reviewer this year. Allowed?

options.label: No: ISQM 2 requires a cooling-off period
Yes: knowledge of the client improves the review
Yes: if the audit committee approves it

explanation: ISQM 2 requires firms to set a cooling-off period (for a listed entity audit, two years) before a former engagement partner can act as engagement quality reviewer.
